BILL NUMBER:S5363

TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the insurance law, in relation to
travel insurance

TITLE: An act to amend the insurance law, in relation to travel
insurance

PURPOSE: This bill would reform the travel agent licensing
requirements in New York to be in accord with the National Association
of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) and National Conference of Insurance
Legislators (NCOII,) models Insurance licensing requirements will be
shifted from the retail travel company and its employees - the vast
majority of whose business emanates from scheduling trips and is not
insurance related - to the travel insurance agent. The travel
insurance agent will be a managing general agent, third party
administrator, or other intermediary working with the insurer and
travel company. Retail travel companies would be registered under the
travel insurance agent's license. The bill also strengthens consumer
protections by adding training requirements for each employee and
authorized representative of the travel company, by clearly
identifying the limited activities in which the travel company is
permitted to engage, and by requiring additional consumer-oriented
disclosures on travel insurance materials.

SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS: Section one of the bill amends the definition
of "limited licensee" in insurance law section 2101 to include a
person authorized to sell travel related products and services

Section two of the bill amends insurance law section 2131 to define
the terms "travel insurance," "travel company", and "travel insurance
agent", along with other travel insurance-related terms The activities
in which travel companies may engage are also clearly defined and
limited. Licensing requirements are shifted from individual retail
travel companies and their employees to travel insurance agents. The
Superintendent of Financial Services is vested with authority to
regulate these agents, including the power to impose monetary fines
and revoke their licenses. New consumer protections include a
requirement to provide a description of the contract terms, the claims
process, and an explanation of the review or cancellation procedure

This section adds a registration requirement compelling travel
insurance agents to maintain a register of each retail travel company
offering travel insurance on its behalf for periodic review by the
Superintendent. This section also inserts a training requirement for
each employee and authorized representative of the travel company.
Topics required to be covered include the types of insurance offered,
ethical sales practices, and required disclosures to prospective
customers.

Section three of the bill amends insurance law section 3452 to
specifically authorize the issuance of a group property travel
insurance policy to a travel company where the policy insures its
travel customers

Section four of the bill provides that the act shall become effective
one hundred and twenty days after becoming a law


JUSTIFICATION: Multi-state licensing of insurance producers has been a
challenging issue for regulators and industry alike for decades. In
response, the NAIC developed the Producer Licensing Model Act (PLMA)
to reflect the licensing reciprocity requirements of the federal
Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act. A majority of states including New York have
adopted all or a portion of the PLMA, putting in place a more
efficient reciprocal licensing framework that enabled producers to
more easily obtain non-resident licenses.

However, these actions have not effectively addressed the practical
challenges associated with multi-state licensing for limited lines
travel insurance. Before states began implementing these reforms,
there were forty-one dissimilar and outdated definitions of travel
insurance across the states, with some still referencing steamships
and other antiquated terms. In an industry that can suffer from high
turnover rates, these roadblocks made licensing reciprocity nearly
impossible.

In New York, travel companies have encountered unique licensing
challenges, causing confusion, delay, and leading to compliance
problems. Naming conflicts between affiliated or similarly-named
companies require some travel companies to change their names or use
fictitious names. In other words, travel agencies, whose principal
business is selling trips and for whom travel insurance is a minute
portion of their business, are forced to change their names or use
fictitious names in order to satisfy a regulatory requirement that is
aimed at more traditional insurance producers. In addition to these
producer licensing issues, travel insurance (which offers a fairly
standard, low-cost benefit package) is addressed within rules not
specifically designed for travel insurance or its current use of group
coverage, creating additional compliance difficulties.

This legislation provides a workable solution to resolve the
regulatory inconsistencies and compliance issues for travel insurance
agents and travel companies. It establishes a licensing framework that
reflects the unique distribution of travel insurance within the travel
industry. Regulatory oversight is strengthened, with burdens
appropriately placed on the travel insurance agent, rather than on the
retail travel company (whose activities are strictly limited to
providing general information, and who is not seeking to act as an
insurance agent). This legislation also dramatically improves consumer
protection by clarifying accountability and requiring notice to the
consumer and the Department of Financial Services with regard to who
is responsible for the sale of travel insurance

In the last three years, 34 states, including California, Texas and
Florida, have implemented very similar legislation, legislation has
been passed and is awaiting governors' signatures in three additional
states, and it is anticipated that most of the remaining states will
implement these standards in the near future The NAIC/NCOIL standards
provide regulators and the travel insurance industry a clearer and
more workable licensing framework for travel insurance, while at the
same time improving consumer protections and disclosures.

LEGISLATIVE HISTORY: New bill.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS: None.


EFFECTIVE DATE: This act shall take effect on the one hundred and
twentieth day after it shall have become a law.
